body.text: Pakistan is set to host the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum 2026 (PMIF-26) in Islamabad on November 12 and 13. The forum will bring together international investors, executives from leading global mining companies, financial institutions, technical experts, and senior government officials to discuss the scope and environment of Pakistan’s mineral sector.

The event is the outcome of similar high-level initiatives in recent years, most notably the first Pakistan Minerals Summit held in August 2023 and subsequent investor forums in 2025. These events have arguably been planned to shift perceptions about Pakistan’s natural resource potential. Moreover, they are aimed at signaling to the international community that the Pakistani state is fully committed to improving investor confidence.
There are three reasons why this forum’s scope and timing are significant, highlighting the strategic trajectory Islamabad is now pursuing regarding its natural resources.

First, the initiative shows that Pakistan recognizes critical minerals as a viable avenue to support national economic growth. At PMIF-26, panels will see participants examining next-generation mining projects, including discoveries from active licenses and strategies for bringing projects into production.

This operational focus at a forum that is fully supported by the government is important. Among other things, it demonstrates that Islamabad is trying to move beyond general exploration and discussions that center merely on the existence of mineral reserves in the country. For instance, by focusing on production schedules, active licensing and early-stage project financing, the Pakistani government seems to be aiming at connecting its resources to global industrial supply chains. Notably, moving from speculative estimates to pitching concrete project management is a key step if the country aims to transform these assets into steady revenue streams in the coming years.

Second, Pakistan’s civil-military leadership appears aligned behind the PIMF initiative. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, senior Cabinet ministers, and top military leaders are expected to attend and address the forum, highlighting a consolidated institutional position. The civil-military alignment on this subject carries political and economic weight for potential investors. For one, it sends a clear message to the international community that there is strong state support and policy continuity. Arguably, capital-intensive sectors like mining require long-term commitment, spanning several decades. In this regard, visible backing from key domestic institutions can go a long way in reassuring foreign companies that the Pakistani state’s support and commitments will remain stable across political shifts in the coming years. Furthermore, this joint front indicates that the state is prepared to carry out necessary legislative, security, and administrative adjustments to streamline approvals and protect long-term investments.

Third, Pakistan has been working to position its mining sector beyond raw material extraction in order to attract foreign direct investment and technical expertise that can support local industrial development. A clear example of this approach is the multi-billion-dollar Reko Diq copper-gold project in Balochistan. The project, which is being developed by Barrick Gold, is a combination of foreign direct investment, technology transfer, and local employment to establish long-term economic capacity rather than a simple extraction deal.

In recent years, Pakistan has been trying to engage international firms and technical experts to evaluate its major reserves, particularly in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. In this regard, forum discussions about logistics and infrastructure connections to regional transport networks offer Pakistan a way to raise the overall competitiveness of its domestic economy. Over time, these frameworks may help lower sovereign risk perceptions and build local operational capacity. This also has the potential to create a direct link between resource development, export revenues and broader economic stability.

More importantly, addressing issues like local stability and security should be a key priority for the Pakistani government in regions where mineral deposits are located. This is important because major mineral deposits are largely concentrated across parts of Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which remain restive. In this regard, providing a safe operational environment, protecting supply routes, and fostering strong community engagement will be essential for building long-term confidence among investors.

While it is encouraging to see high-level events like PMIF-26 demonstrating unified support across state institutions, the long-term success of this effort will depend on factors beyond government backing. Pakistan can benefit more if steady structural reforms are implemented and political stability is perceived by foreign investors as a continuous factor beyond the current government.

While high-level forums can open doors, foreign investors also look for long-term stability. It is precisely this stable environment that Pakistan’s civil-military leadership is increasingly keen to demonstrate.

Moreover, converting investor interest into multi-decade capital deployment requires deep institutional predictability. This is a reality that government stakeholders in Pakistan are likely aware of as they work toward broader sectoral implementation. It will be interesting to watch how Pakistan navigates the commercial and operational opportunities these plans bring.
